item.title: Makkah Pact: FM says no reason for anyone to be upset or worried
item.description:
Foreign Minister Dr Khalilur Rahman on Sunday reiterated that the "Makkah Pact" is an internal matter of the world Muslim family and that there is no reason for anyone to be upset or worried about this.
“This is not a matter of threatening. This is not a matter of attacking anyone. This is a matter of self-defense of our world Muslim family. So I do not see any reason for anyone to be upset or worried about this,” he said.
Dr Khalilur left Dhaka on Sunday night for New York to take up his responsibilities as president of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly, a tenure that will coincide with a crucial period for the world body, including the selection of a new UN secretary-general.
The foreign minister left Dhaka shortly after 8:20pm on an official visit to New York, US, in connection with his UNGA presidency from August 31 to October 21 and is scheduled to transit through Dubai, a senior official told UNB.
Asked about possible challenges in discharging the two responsibilities, Dr Khalilur said diplomats deal with realities rather than hypothetical situations.
“Look, we are diplomats. We do not work on ‘ifs’. We work on reality,” he told private television channel "Independent TV" in an interview before leaving Dhaka for New York.
The 81st session of the General Assembly will formally open on September 8, with world leaders expected to gather at UN Headquarters in New York later in the month for the annual high-level general debate.
The foreign minister said Bangladesh will maintain good relations with all countries while firmly protecting its national interests, reiterating that the government’s foreign policy is guided by the principle of “Bangladesh First.”
“Bangladesh First” means that Bangladesh is not alone. It means that we will maintain our relations by ensuring our mutual interests,” he said.
Dr Khalilur, who is set to serve as president of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, said he does not anticipate any major difficulty in handling the two responsibilities simultaneously.
He said another state minister has been appointed to the Foreign Ministry and that he has worked closely with the minister.
“So I do not see any particular challenge in performing my duties,” he said.
Dr Khalilur said the Rohingya crisis and the broader issue of refugees and displaced people would be among his priorities as President of the UN General Assembly.
“Refugees, displaced people, these are part of my priorities. I said that during my election. So I will definitely have a strong eye on this,” he said.
The issue would receive special attention during the UN General Assembly’s High-Level Week beginning September 22.
“There will be a high-level side event and I will present my statement there as President of the General Assembly,” he said.
Dr Khalilur reiterated Bangladesh’s longstanding position that repatriation is the only sustainable solution to the Rohingya crisis.
“There is only one solution to this problem - repatriation,” he said.
Dr Khalilur noted that the position has now gained broad international recognition and that even the Myanmar government has acknowledged the issue, although Bangladesh disagrees with some of the figures provided by Myanmar.
“Not everything in diplomacy is done publicly. Most of it is done behind the scenes. And when there is a success or failure, you see it face to face,” he said.
Assuming the presidency at a time of deepening geopolitical divisions, the Foreign Minister has pledged to make consensus-building and restoring confidence in the UN central to his tenure.
“The UN will commence its ninth decade at a time when trust in our organization is being tested on multiple fronts,” Dr Khalilur told UN member states.
He said the challenges facing the international community were undermining public trust and confidence in the UN’s ability to deliver on its commitments.
“As your president, I will dedicate myself to rebuilding trust, nurturing consensus, and opening space for good-faith negotiations that will lead to outcomes for all that are owned by all,” he said.
Dr Khalilur has also pledged to serve as a bridge-builder among member states, engage all sides, and work to find common ground amid widening divisions.
He said he would uphold the UN Charter and ensure geographical and gender balance within the Office of the President of the General Assembly while remaining attentive to the needs of smaller delegations.
Bangladesh is also expected to use the high-profile presidency to advance issues of national and regional importance, particularly the protracted Rohingya crisis.
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam recently said Dhaka hopes to use its stronger diplomatic position at the UN to intensify international pressure on Myanmar and build momentum for a political and durable solution to the crisis.
“We are trying to involve the international community more,” she said, referring to a high-level UN session on the Rohingya crisis expected to be held in September, with Bangladesh’s Prime Minister Tarique Rahman expected to participate.
Shama Obaed said Dhaka hopes the high-level discussion will produce clearer international guidelines and stronger momentum towards resolving the crisis, which has become increasingly complex amid security and other challenges.
Bangladesh has repeatedly called for sustained international engagement to ensure the safe, voluntary, and dignified return of the Rohingya to Myanmar, while seeking greater global support for addressing the humanitarian and security dimensions of the crisis.

item.title: Mirza Fakhrul’s real test will come in 2031
item.description:
When the Constitution of Bangladesh was amended in 1991 and the parliamentary system was reinstated, the then interim president is said to have made an interesting observation.
Seeing that virtually all the powers of the president had been taken away by the amendment, Justice Shahabuddin Ahmed remarked: “The president will now have no other work to do except visit the shrines.”
However, it cannot be said that all presidents have been able to visit shrines peacefully.
In Bangladesh’s deeply divided political landscape, a deceased leader is sometimes feared more than a living one.
In 2002, the BNP forced its own nominated president, Badruddoza Chowdhury, to resign after only seven months in office. His crime? He had expressed a desire to visit the grave of Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman. Some say, however, that president Chowdhury had expressed reluctance to visit the grave of former president Ziaur Rahman, the founder of the BNP.
Whatever the truth, Badruddoza Chowdhury had to leave Bangabhaban in disgrace amid the controversy over which grave he would or would not visit.
The present is not free of controversy either.
Many had expected the new Parliament to do two things at the beginning of its session: Establish an upper house with 105 members, and then elect a new president through a vote of the members of both houses.
The debate over how members of the upper house would be elected, according to the proportion of votes received in the general election or the proportion of seats won in the lower house, ended with the BNP’s absolute victory.
Meanwhile, some significant changes to the powers of the president are also expected, if the “July Charter” is indeed a meaningful document for the BNP.
Caretaker is coming
However, even before all this, a new president was elected on August 20.
There has hardly been any adverse reaction to the person elected.
It would not be wrong to say that Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir is one of the most experienced and respected politicians not only in the BNP but also in Bangladesh.
He visited the grave of Ziaur Rahman but expressed no desire to visit the grave of Bangabandhu. He has passed the initial test of survival. But the discussion over the future of the presidency has not ended with this election, it may only have begun.
Why Awami League-nominated Md Sahabuddin remained president for six months even after the BNP secured a two-thirds majority in the election is also a matter of curiosity and deserves analysis.
There is little doubt that Mirza Fakhrul’s work as president will largely be limited to formalities. But even if the president has nothing to do for the next four and a half years except “visit the shrines,” the final six months will be eventful.
Under the current system, elections must be held within 90 days before the expiry of Parliament’s term. In other words, Parliament remains in session during the election.
But the High Court has already reinstated the system of holding elections under a non-partisan, impartial caretaker government. All that remains is to determine the process for selecting the chief adviser and other members of the caretaker government and to incorporate the necessary amendments into the Constitution.
In principle, Bangladesh’s 2031 general election will be held under a caretaker government.
Biswas to Iazuddin
A feature of the caretaker system is that the prime minister will request the president in writing to dissolve Parliament only after the existing Parliament has completed its full five-year term.
The government will also resign, and the chief adviser of the caretaker government will take the oath of office and begin work.
The president will play a major role during this period, as he will be the only elected officeholder, the commander-in-chief of the armed forces, and the wheels of the bureaucracy will turn on his orders.
Here, one can look back to 2001.
Justice Latifur Rahman made 13 secretaries OSD within an hour of taking office as chief adviser on July 15.
His move created a stir in political circles. There was strong suspicion within the Awami League, the party that had just left power, that Justice Rahman would work against it.
But the fact is that the new chief adviser sidelined secretaries appointed by the Awami League in order to work impartially. He did not do this alone. He acted in consultation with the then president, Justice Shahabuddin Ahmed.
Two other instances can be recalled. First, Justice Habibur Rahman took over as chief adviser after the caretaker system was introduced in 1996. But when Army Chief General Mohammad Nasim tried to seize power, some senior officers helped President Abdur Rahman Biswas at Bangabhaban foil the coup attempt.
Second, in 2006, the ruling BNP tried to secure a chief adviser of its choice by increasing the retirement age of judges. After this attempt to manipulate the caretaker system failed, BNP-nominated President Iazuddin Ahmed declared himself chief adviser.
Many suspected at the time that President Ahmed was acting in consultation with the recently departed prime minister, Khaleda Zia. But that attempt to influence the election also failed when Iazuddin Ahmed, under pressure from the army, declared a state of emergency and postponed the election.
Md Sahabuddin’s disrespect
Against this diverse and turbulent backdrop, Mirza Fakhrul will face a test of impartiality and integrity. The country’s next election will be held within three months of the end of the 13th Parliament.
Those three months will be the most important and consequential period of Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir’s presidency.
The date of the presidential election, the 20th of this month, appears to have been carefully chosen. The respect Tarique Rahman showed President Md Sahabuddin does not appear to have been mere courtesy.
Sahabuddin once complained that the chief adviser of the interim government had shown him no respect at all and had instead humiliated him. He wanted to resign at the time. But, overwhelmed by Tarique Rahman’s respect, he remained in office.
Six months later, the BNP government forced President Md Sahabuddin to resign. There did not appear to be much respect on display then. He was not even invited to the swearing-in ceremony of the new president.
With the presidential election taking place six months after the formation of Parliament, Mirza Fakhrul’s term will expire in August 2031. That means he will remain in this crucial position throughout the entire election period under the caretaker government.
What kind of role will he play? Can he rise above his loyalty to the party and play a neutral role in the interests of the country?
Mirza Fakhrul’s answer is “yes.”
He has resigned from all BNP posts and announced that he has severed his ties with the party. He has said that he will now act impartially.
Maladaptive political culture
It is certainly reassuring to hear Mirza Fakhrul’s words, and ordinary people will hope that he can act accordingly.
But they also know how difficult it is to play a genuinely “neutral” role in Bangladesh’s bitter and vindictive political culture.
For example, it is practically impossible to deny Sheikh Mujib’s place in Bangladesh’s independence struggle and political history. But will Mirza Fakhrul be able to acknowledge this truth in any of his speeches? If he can, it will be a sign of his political wisdom and maturity -- and, perhaps more importantly, that of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman.
People will not expect the impossible from the president. No one will expect him to go beyond his constitutional limitations and perform some miracle.
They will simply expect the president to make it easier for his chief adviser to uphold the central principle of the caretaker government system, ensuring a free and fair election.
However, it is also true that no president has so far been able to overturn an election. Since the caretaker system was incorporated into the Constitution, three elections have been held under this arrangement.
Two were conducted under BNP-nominated presidents, and Khaleda Zia’s party was defeated in both.
The election held under an Awami League-nominated president resulted in disaster for Sheikh Hasina.
What the situation will look like in 2031, however, is difficult to predict.
Sabir Mustafa is former head of BBC Bangla and is currently working as a freelance journalist and podcaster. Views expressed are the writer’s own.

item.title: 'Friendship' founder Runa Khan wins Ramon Magsaysay Award
item.description:
Runa Khan, founder of Friendship, has been named a recipient of the 2026 Ramon Magsaysay Award for her more than two decades of leadership in developing locally led solutions that empower marginalised communities to live with greater opportunity, dignity and hope.
The Ramon Magsaysay Award is Asia’s premier prize and highest honour—widely regarded as “Asia's Nobel Prize”, recognising “greatness of spirit” and “transformative leadership in Asia”.
Runa Khan is the 14th recipient of the Award from Bangladesh, after, in particular, Muhammad Yunus, founder of Grameen and Mother Teresa from India, both of whom also received the Nobel Prize for Peace. Incidentally, Mother Teresa had travelled to Bangladesh in the nineties and blessed the river barge that would later become Friendship’s first hospital ship. Other outstanding awardees have also been the Fazle Hasan Abed, founder of Brac, the Dalai Lama and Japanese filmmaker Akira Kurasawa. The formal award ceremony will be held on 15 November in Manila, Philippines. On receiving the award, Runa Khan said: “It is with great happiness and profound humility that I accept the Ramon Magsaysay Award. There is no leader who walks alone, so it is an honour for me to receive this on behalf of the unaddressed communities, who allow us to walk beside them; and on behalf of my Friendship family whose tireless devotion makes this work possible every day. I thank also those who have trusted and walked this almost impossible path with me for 25 long years—just believing. My children whose patience and understanding awes me. This recognition is a wonderful responsibility, and I offer my deepest gratitude to the Ramon Magsaysay Award Foundation for their trust and for honouring the enduring faith and power of humanity.” For Runa Khan, the recognition honours a body of work that began in Bangladesh’s remote riverine communities and grew into an integrated model for delivering solutions based on a deep understanding and respect of local communities and their realities. What began with a single floating hospital has grown into a social purpose organisation serving 7.5 million people annually across healthcare, education, climate action, sustainable economic development, inclusive citizenship and cultural preservation. Its holistic approach reflects the interconnected challenges faced by remote communities. Under strong leadership, Friendship’s approach is simple: systems should be designed around people’s realities rather than expecting people to fit systems that cannot reach them. It recruits and trains local people and works with communities to shape the solutions meant for them, taking an inclusive approach by involving women and people with disabilities and connecting health, education, livelihoods, rights and climate resilience. Five years after founding Friendship in Bangladesh, Runa Khan took the initiative to establish Friendship in Luxembourg in 2006, Netherlands in 2007, the UK in 2010, France in 2015, and Belgium in 2018. Her vision was to work as closely as possible with donors and creating partners, thereby bypassing the long chains of intermediaries in international aid while preserving local ownership. That vision has proven to be extremely effective thanks to a strong community of supporters, both public and private. The International entities have stood by the side of Friendship Bangladesh at every stage of its development over the past 24 years.
In her official Ramon Magsaysay Award citation, Runa Khan is being recognised for “her profound empathy for the poorest of the poor in her country, and her courage, vision, and tenacity in building and leading Friendship to accomplish her mission. In her hands, privilege became not an entitlement, but a responsibility; not a family legacy to protect, but a gift to be shared so that others, too, might have the chance to live with hope, opportunity, and dignity.” The Ramon Magsaysay Award was first given in 1958 in memory of the seventh Philippine President Ramon Magsaysay.
In 68 years, the Award has been bestowed on 328 individuals and 28 organisations whose selfless service has offered their societies in 24 countries across Asia, and the rest of the world solutions to some of the most challenging problems of human development.

item.title: The uncomfortable truth for young men
item.description:
Looking out from behind a senior sub editor’s desk after 14 years in newsrooms, I often catch myself watching the latest wave of SSC and HSC candidates celebrating their results.
They smile for photos, full of idealism and relief, unaware of the silent shift waiting just around the corner.
Every time I see them, my mind wanders back to the young boy I once was -- standing in those exact same shoes, making the exact same dangerous assumptions about time, money, and responsibility.
If I could reach back through the decades, pull my younger self aside, and spare him from the quiet stumbles of my youth, this is the unvarnished truth I would tell him.
Look at how softly the world treats you right now. You make mistakes, and people smile.
You fail, and you are offered grace.
But listen to me carefully: That cushion is about to evaporate.
Society will soon measure your worth not by your good intentions, but by your utility and the weight of your pocket.
I made the mistake of assuming that affection was permanent. It isn't.
A jobless, directionless man -- a bekar purush -- commands no real respect, whether in extended family circles, among peers, or in the wider world.
Three anchors you cannot ignore
I spent years prioritizing the wrong things in the wrong order. If you want to build a life that stands firm when storms hit, you need three things, strictly in this order:
Build these three early, and you will step miles ahead of the crowd.
There were times when I saw people taking shady shortcuts, wondering if sticking strictly to pure means was keeping me behind. It was a lie.
Anyone who tells you that you cannot build substantial wealth through halal avenues is merely justifying their own moral compromises.
The real battle you will face isn't finding halal work -- it is having the discipline to turn down fast, attractive opportunities.
Walk away from every questionable deal, no matter how tempting.
‘Later’ is the biggest lie you will tell yourself
I used to tell myself: "I'll focus on earning after A Levels," and then, "I'll worry about real skills after university." That hesitation cost me years.
A framed certificate is not a magic key. No employer, no investor, and no client is going to hand you money simply because you held up a degree on graduation day.
If you wait until you finish institutional milestones to start learning how the real world works, you are already dangerously late.
Start gaining practical knowledge today. Tomorrow is an illusion.
Degree is not a strategy
Look closely at the university graduates around you. How many of them actually achieved their dreams solely because of the paper they received?
Now sit in the chair I sit in today -- as a team leader.
If two people walk into my office for a position, and one spent four years reading outdated theory while the other spent four years building real-world skills and executing projects, I will pick the practitioner every single time.
Unless you are becoming a doctor or an engineer, do not treat a degree as your core strategy.
Value comes from execution, not enrollment.
I used to think that life required choosing between worldly success and spiritual devotion. That was a false dichotomy.
Getting married and building a home seems daunting in our culture, but it becomes effortless when you build yourself into a trustworthy, responsible, and stable man.
I have seen wealthy men who neglect their prayers and indulge in corruption; society uses them for money but despises their character. On the flip side, I have seen bright young men stay in the mosque all day, possessing beautiful manners, yet unable to spare Tk100 for a necessity because they refused to build a livelihood.
Be gentle and approachable, but stay firm when your principles are tested.
Your physical and mental window is closing
Right now, you think you have infinite time. You don't. Today, you are labeled a "student."
Almost overnight, that label shifts to "unemployed."
At 14, 18, or 20, your energy is a superpower.
You can sleep four hours, learn a complex skill, work a shift, and recover instantly.
A few years down the line, that raw stamina wanes, your cognitive processing slows, and life demands higher stakes for every error.
The world forgives a teenager's mistakes; it penalizes an adult for the exact same ones.
Use your peak energy right now while the stakes are low and the grace period is still open.
Achieving something at 21 hits entirely differently than achieving it at 31.
When you achieve independence early, society notices. The doors open wider, and the trajectory of your entire life shifts upward.
Protect your name at all costs
In 14 years of professional life, I have seen careers built on reputation and destroyed by the lack of it. Your name is your currency.
Be the young man in your neighborhood, among your friends' parents, and in your institution who is known as safe, reliable, and honourable.
A reputation takes years of quiet consistency to build and seconds of foolishness to ruin.
The formula is simple: High skill, clean income, excellent manners, and absolute reliability.
If you say you will do something, do it -- no excuses.
If there is one profound lesson my career in media has hammered into me, it is this: Speed of execution beats perfection every single time.
If you decide today to learn a skill, do not plan for next month -- start the foundation before the sun sets today.
If you want to build a public voice or a service, have your first draft, post, or offer live within hours.
Move fast. Moving fast means you fail faster, learn faster, and correct course faster.
I wasted too much time waiting for the "right moment" or waiting for life to change on its own.
Life never changes on its own. You have to grab the steering wheel and force the turn yourself.
Stop waiting. Your future self depends on what you do before you go to sleep tonight.
Wafiur Rahman looks after the business desk at Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: Hamza closes in on Sheffield United return
item.description:
Bangladesh midfielder Hamza Choudhury is closing in on a permanent return to Sheffield United, with the Championship club reportedly set to bring him back from Leicester City before the transfer window closes.
English media reports on Sunday said the 28-year-old is poised to leave Leicester, with Sheffield United emerging as his likely destination. Leicester Mercury reported that Hamza is closing in on a permanent move to the Blades.
Hamza is already familiar with Sheffield United, having spent the second half of the 2024-25 season at Bramall Lane on loan from Leicester. He made 16 Championship appearances during that spell and became an important member of the squad as the club challenged for promotion.
The Bangladesh international returned to Leicester following his loan spell and remained with his boyhood club. However, Leicester's relegation to League One has opened the door for a move, with Sheffield United now looking to reunite with the versatile midfielder.
The move could be completed imminently, with Hamza reportedly expected to undergo a medical ahead of the Championship transfer deadline on Tuesday night.
Hamza, who primarily plays as a defensive midfielder, came through Leicester's academy and has made more than 100 appearances for the Foxes.

item.title: Transforming Chittagong’s port capacity
item.description:
The planned $550 million Laldia Terminal is one of the most ambitious port projects Bangladesh has taken on - one that has the potential to reshape Chittagong.
A modern terminal with expanded capacity, efficient cargo handling, and improved connectivity is exactly what we need to keep pace with rising export volumes and global shipping demands. Above all else, this is what we need as Bangladesh looks to take the meaningful next step in its development journey.
Done right, this could become a cornerstone of Bangladesh’s economic future, but ambition alone is not enough. We have seen too many large infrastructure projects suffer from delays, cost overruns, and coordination failures. The Laldia Terminal cannot afford to join that list.
Given that the port is projected to be made entirely with foreign investment, there is an even greater need to ensure this is done right. Foreign investment continues to be a challenge for our nation, and ensuring the port development stays on track is one way to instil confidence into future investors.
As such, this project must be executed with discipline: Strict adherence to timelines, transparent procurement, and rigorous oversight.
Moreover, future development for Bangladesh must be built upon the principles of sustainability, with a clear operational plan that ensures projects deliver the benefits promised.
If implemented properly, the terminal will strengthen Bangladesh’s position in global supply chains, support export‑led growth, and ease the strain on existing port facilities. It is a project that can genuinely transform Chittagong -- but only if it is treated with the urgency it deserves and not yet another slow‑moving development scheme.
Bangladesh needs this terminal. Now it must prove it can deliver it -- on time, on budget, and with the seriousness our future demands.

item.title: Promises on e‑rickshaw regulation mean nothing without action
item.description:
The government moving to bring e-rickshaws under a policy framework, with systematic licensing and registration planned through local government, is unquestionably a positive development - on paper.
However, Bangladesh has heard this promise before.
For some time now, authorities have announced plans to register, regulate, and reorganize these vehicles, only for the initiatives to stall, fade, or be quietly abandoned.
This time, the country needs more than statements. It needs implementation.
E‑rickshaws are now an essential part of Bangladesh’s transport ecosystem and play a significant role in providing affordable mobility in addition to creating livelihoods for hundreds of thousands. None of this has ever been disputed.
Yet, their rapid, unregulated growth coupled with their high-risk has also created serious problems. Untrained drivers should never have been allowed to operate these vehicles, and it is no wonder that Dhaka has seen increased traffic chaos and more frequent accidents.
Without proper oversight, a mode of transport that should help communities has unfortunately ended up putting them at risk, not to mention worsen our traffic woes.
The government’s renewed commitment to registration, route management, and safety standards is therefore welcome - but credibility depends entirely on follow‑through.
We expect the government to realize why past attempts failed and not give in to coercion from vested interests resisting change. Unless these structural issues are addressed, this latest initiative will meet the same fate.
Bangladesh cannot afford another cycle of announcements without action. E‑rickshaws are here to stay and the goal now is to transform them from the source of disorder they are today to becoming a safe, integrated part of the transport system.

item.title: DPDC clarifies prepaid meter charges, ghost bills; urges customers to call 16116
item.description:
The Dhaka Power Distribution Company Limited (DPDC) has urged customers facing abnormal electricity bills, billing discrepancies or unexpected power disconnections to contact its customer service centers or call the hotline 16116 for prompt assistance.
The call comes amid complaints and concerns from customers over deductions of various charges during prepaid meter recharges, unusually high or “ghost” bills, power disconnections at midnight or on holidays, and unusually long tokens generated during the first recharge after a tariff change.
In a notice issued on Monday, DPDC explained different charges and procedures related to prepaid meters and electricity bills to address customers’ concerns and reduce their inconvenience.
It said a demand charge is deducted once a month against the sanctioned load. If a customer does not recharge in a particular month, the demand charges for the months without vending, along with the charge for the current month, are deducted when a customer recharges next.
DPDC said the demand charge also applies to postpaid customers.
Regarding meter rent, the company said no rent is applicable if customers purchase and install their own prepaid meters. If a meter is supplied by DPDC, a monthly rent of Tk 40 applies for a single-phase meter and Tk 250 for a three-phase meter.
A 5% VAT is deducted from the amount recharged each time, in line with the government-set rate applicable to electricity bills.
DPDC said a 200–220-digit token may be generated during the first recharge after a tariff change to activate the new tariff in prepaid meters.
It said this is due to the technical features of the meters and the multiple slabs under different electricity tariff categories.
However, the long token is required only for the first recharge after a tariff change. Subsequent recharges continue to use the usual 20-digit token.
DPDC said it has taken an initiative to bring prepaid meters online to resolve the inconvenience caused by entering long tokens manually.
AMI prepaid meters are currently being installed, which do not require tokens and can be easily recharged through online platforms, including bKash and Rocket.
DPDC said there is no scope for prepaid meters to deduct charges exceeding actual electricity consumption or generate so-called “ghost bills.”
According to the company, the cost of electricity is deducted gradually based on actual consumption and the retail electricity tariff fixed by the Bangladesh Energy Regulatory Commission (BERC).
It said abnormal billing should not occur in prepaid meters unless there is a technical fault, including a common-neutral-related problem.
DPDC said electricity supply is not disconnected even if the prepaid meter balance runs out during weekly holidays or “friendly hours”, defined as 4pm to 10am the following day.
During this period, the meter continues to supply electricity with a negative balance, which is adjusted during the next recharge.
Customers can also activate an emergency balance after their energy balance runs out, allowing them to continue using electricity in emergencies. The amount is subsequently adjusted during the next recharge.
DPDC said customers should not panic if they experience abnormal deductions, billing discrepancies or power disconnections at unexpected times due to technical problems.
Customers are advised to contact the relevant customer service or complaint center, or call DPDC’s hotline at 16116, providing their meter number, customer number and other necessary information.
The company said complaints will be properly verified and, where applicable, necessary corrections and remedial measures will be taken promptly.

item.title: President stresses stronger BGB role in preventing border killings, smuggling
item.description:
President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir on Monday stressed the need for stronger role by Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) to prevent smuggling, drug trafficking, push-ins and border killings.
He made the call when BGB Director General Major General Mohammad Ashrafuzzaman Siddiqui paid a courtesy call on the president at Bangabhaban.
During the meeting, the BGB DG congratulated President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir on assuming office.
He briefed him on the force’s overall activities and initiatives to enhance surveillance along the borders through the deployment of advanced drones and modern technologies.
President Fakhrul appreciated the BGB’s initiative to introduce advanced technologies to strengthen border security and assured the force of all-out cooperation in this regard.
The president’s secretaries and senior officials were present during the meeting.

item.title: Campaign launched against battery-run autorickshaws in Dhaka-13
item.description:
Authorities have launched a campaign against the illegal operation of battery-run autorickshaws and unauthorised battery-charging establishments in Dhaka-13 following complaints from local residents.
The campaign was launched on Monday on the instructions of State Minister for Primary and Mass Education and Dhaka-13 MP Bobby Hajjaj, according to a press release issued by the ministry.
The press release said residents raised complaints about traffic congestion and the unrestricted movement of battery-run autorickshaws at a town hall meeting in the constituency on Saturday.
Taking the matter seriously, Bobby Hajjaj instructed the relevant authorities to take immediate action.
The campaign began on Sunday, during which authorities took action against a number of battery-run autorickshaws and removed equipment and electrical connections used for unauthorised battery charging.
The initiative aims to restore order on the roads and ensure smoother movement of people in the area, the press release said.
Bobby Hajjaj said the town hall meeting was not merely a platform for hearing complaints but also an effective way to identify citizens’ problems and provide quick solutions.
“We have immediately instructed the relevant authorities to address the issues raised by residents,” he said.
He said necessary measures would continue to ensure normal and smooth movement in Dhaka-13.
The state minister also said coordination between the administration and relevant organisations would be strengthened to address residents’ concerns.
“Work is underway to make Dhaka-13 a more liveable and people-friendly area by giving importance to citizens’ complaints and suggestions,” he said.
Local residents expressed satisfaction with the swift action following their complaints at the town hall meeting, according to the press release.

item.title: Bellingham, Mbappe fire as Real ease to Malaga win
item.description:
Jude Bellingham and Kylian Mbappe both struck as Real Madrid's perfect start to La Liga under Jose Mourinho continued in a 4-0 cruise against Malaga on Sunday.
Los Blancos scored three times in just over 10 minutes in the first half to open up a comfortable lead over the Andalusian visitors to the Santiago Bernabeu.
Sandwiched between Bellingham and Mbappe's strikes was an own goal by Malaga goalkeeper Alfonso Herrero, while Arda Guler tapped in a fourth late on.
"I've got the freedom to go higher or lower if we need, I'm enjoying myself a lot," Bellingham told Real Madrid TV of his attacking midfield role under Mourinho.
The former Birmingham and Borussia Dortmund star was given a standing ovation from the fans when he was substituted in the second half.
"It's an honour to play for this club and in front of these fans and the ovation was very nice," added Bellingham.
After two victories in their opening two games and with superstar trio Mbappe, Bellingham and Vinicius Junior starting the season well, Madrid's confidence was high.
Mourinho rotated, making five changes to the team that started their opening matches, giving Trent Alexander-Arnold and Marc Cucurella among others their first starts this season.
Bellingham opened the scoring after 19 minutes with an excellent solo goal, beating two defenders before drilling through Herrero's legs.
Bellingham forced the second goal seven minutes later, after Herrero denied Mbappe.
The England international headed the rebound towards goal and defender Carlos Puga desperately tried to clear off the line, with the ball bouncing in off the unfortunate stopper Herrero.
Mbappe rattled home the third with a volley from Alexander-Arnold's cross for his fourth goal of the campaign, leaving him top of Spain's scoring charts.
Promoted side Malaga threatened just before half-time, with Rafa Rodriguez striking the post after a corner was played to him, and Chupe hitting the side netting.
- Clean sheet banked -
Madrid cruised through the second half, with Bellingham hitting the outside of the post as they occasionally threatened to extend their lead.
They only managed to get a fourth late on, when Vinicius teed up substitute Guler to finish from point-blank range.
"The second half was more about managing the game, at a lower tempo," Mourinho told Real Madrid TV.
"Malaga were calmer on the ball, but every time we stepped up the pace, it always felt like we could score one or two more.
"One of our objectives was to keep a clean sheet."
Madrid managed to do that for the first time this season and Mourinho said it was important for Los Blancos.
"Football isn't just about having fun with the beauty of the goals -- it's also about going home thinking that we're a solid unit," added the Portuguese veteran.
Deportivo La Coruna secured their first win of the season with a 3-1 victory over Valencia.
Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang netted his third goal of the campaign for the Galician side, who also benefitted from own goals by Cesar Tarrega and Mouctar Diakhaby.
Edin Terzic's Athletic Bilbao also claimed their first win, 2-0 at Celta Vigo, with goals from Alex Berenguer and Robert Navarro.
On Monday, champions Barcelona host Rayo Vallecano in their third match of the campaign, having comfortably won their opening games.

item.title: FIFA president Infantino 'must go', says ex-UEFA boss Platini
item.description:
French football great Michel Platini said on Sunday FIFA president Gianni Infantino "must go" following the scandals that have rocked world football's governing body.
The 56-year-old Infantino has been under fire since his aborted plan to bring private investment into FIFA events, such as the World Cup.
He was also lambasted over a number of controversies during the recently-ended World Cup in North America.
"Economic affairs are one thing but Infantino has failed because he is the guarantor of the rules of the game and he didn't respect them," former UEFA president Platini told Canal+.
Platini hit out at the so-called hydration breaks at the World Cup, which often lasted as much as four minutes and were used by the host broadcaster for advertisements.
He also pointed to the half-time show during the final which largely overran the required maximum of 15 minutes, and the furore around FIFA suspending the red card ban given to American forward Folarin Balogun following a phone call made by US President Donald Trump to Infantino.
"The ad breaks are not in the rules, the 30-minute half-time break in the final is not in the rules, and the red card, that's the worst," said Platini.
"He's the guarantor (of the rules), he doesn't respect them, he must go," added Platini about Infantino, who was UEFA's secretary general under the Frenchman's leadership.
Since the World Cup, UEFA threatened to boycott FIFA tournaments until Infantino scrapped the FIFA Forward Enterprises plan to bring in private investment.
European football's governing body UEFA has also accused Infantino of "criminal mismanagement" over the private financing.
- 'He always loved money' -
Other regions, CONCACAF and Asia, have joined UEFA in putting pressure on Infantino, who is hoping to run for re-election in March.
"It won't be sporting institutions that sort this out and bring him down," Platini said.
"If UEFA wanta to bring down Infantino, it will be through the courts."
"I always knew that he loved money and power," Platini added about the Swiss-Italian.
Platini was himself accused of fraud in 2015 when he was UEFA president and eyeing the top job at FIFA to replace Sepp Blatter, who was likewise accused of giving an illegal 2-million-dollar payment to the Frenchman.
Platini was eventually acquitted of any wrongdoing in 2025 but was forced to step down at the time, with Infantino leaping on the opportunity to be elected FIFA president in his stead in 2016.
"He didn't bring me down, he benefitted from it," said Platini.
"But now that there are lots of investigations into him all over the world, there is some noise about how he knew about certain things -- let's see what happens next."
Platini is suing Infantino, and former FIFA officials Marco Villiger and Domenico Scala, in France "to seek compensation for all the damages he has suffered as a result of the tactics used to prevent him from being elected FIFA President in 2015".
He accuses the trio of a "criminal conspiracy to commit false accusation... influence peddling... and aiding and abetting influence peddling".

item.title: Calhanoglu fires Inter to nervy Cagliari win, Como stun Napoli
item.description:
Hakan Calhanoglu's early strike earned Inter Milan a 1-0 win at Cagliari on Sunday as they continued a perfect start to their Serie A title defence, while Como edged Napoli 2-1 to spoil Massimiliano Allegri's home debut.
Turkey midfielder Calhanoglu guided home a first-time strike from the edge of the box after nine minutes to make it two goals in two games and set the tone for a first half dominated by the champions in Sardinia.
A combination of wayward finishing and fine goalkeeping from Elia Caprile kept the scoreline close at half-time, and Inter's profligacy continued after the break as Lautaro Martinez, Francesco Pio Esposito and Alessandro Bastoni squandered good chances.
England international Curtis Jones made his debut from the bench in the second half, but Inter's lack of composure in front of goal almost came back to bite them as Cagliari threatened a shock equaliser with a flurry of late chances.
Cristian Chivu's side ended the game with 29 shots on the board and only one goal to show for them, but it was enough to send them top of the table after two games, ahead of AC Milan, Juventus and Lazio on goal difference.
"These are your classic games where if you don't close them out, you can run into trouble," Chivu told Sky Italia.
"In the last few minutes, we fell apart, getting confused and panicking.
"But we held firm, and we created a lot. If there is one regret, it is not finishing off the many chances we had."
Gennaro Gattuso's Lazio also made it two wins from two by beating Genoa 1-0 in Rome thanks to a second match-winning strike in a row from summer signing Davide Frattesi.
- Fabregas hopes for striker -
Earlier, Como pulled off their latest feat of Serie A giant-killing as a win at the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona ruined Napoli coach Allegri's home bow.
Martin Baturina fired Cesc Fabregas's enterprising side into a deserved lead in the 17th minute as chances fell at both ends in soaring temperatures in Naples.
Rasmus Hojlund's brilliant strike drew the hosts level on the half-hour mark, but his good work was quickly undone when a defensive mix-up led to Anastasios Douvikas scoring for the second game in a row.
Kevin De Bruyne, who inspired Napoli to an opening win over Genoa with a goal and assist from the bench, was unable to turn the tide after coming on early in the second half.
Como survived late pressure to hold on as Stanislav Lobotka's stoppage-time strike was ruled out for offside.
"It is a very valuable win... the first half was very good and in the second we understood that we were facing champions, and we held out," Fabregas told broadcasters DAZN.
Fabregas's side upset the established order in Italian football last season by qualifying for the Champions League for the first time, where they were drawn against the likes of holders Paris Saint-Germain, Barcelona and Manchester United.
But the Spanish coach admitted that he is hoping for more new signings before the transfer window closes on September 1, to help cope with a busy schedule.
"Obviously, I'm expecting a striker," Fabregas said.
"Douvikas can't play both the league and the cups. We suffered a lot with (Alvaro) Morata last year, for months he was out injured.
"Playing every three days at this level isn't easy."
Como, who were held by Udinese in their opener, moved up to four points, while last season's runners-up Napoli remained on three points.
The second round of the Serie A season concludes on Monday when Roma travel to Lecce before Atalanta host Bologna.

item.title: Monaco beat Marseille to go top, Rosenior's Paris FC thump Nice
item.description:
Monaco stormed to the top of Ligue 1 with a 2-0 win over Marseille on Sunday as former Chelsea boss Lionel Rosenior led his new charges Paris FC to a 3-0 home thumping of Nice.
German Paris Brunner scored both goals as Monaco maintained the only remaining perfect record in Ligue 1 after two matches.
"Since I joined, he's been the type of player who expresses himself on the pitch, in training, with goals, pressing, tracking back -- he wants to learn," said Monaco coach Filipe Luis about his match-winner.
"That's the way he is. It's all up to him if he wants to keep doing his talking on the pitch.
"As long as he keeps doing that, he'll be there. He's very young, I'm really happy with the way he played.
"But the most important thing is that he remains ambitious, passionate, because he is passionate when he plays and I love that."
The 20-year-old opened the scoring on 13 minutes with a header from captain Aleksandr Golovin's cross from the right.
Nine minutes after half-time, he cut inside Marseille centre-backs Geoffrey Kondogbia and CJ Egan-Riley before shooting past goalkeeper Jeffrey De Lange.
In the capital, newly-recruited Malian striker Lassine Sinayoko broke the deadlock from the penalty-spot on 20 minutes.
Samir Chergui doubled that after a blistering counter-attack after 51 minutes, while Vincent Marchetti pounced on a loose ball late on to make it 3-0 to PFC.
Former Strasbourg boss Rosenior was brought back to France following his torrid experience at Chelsea by the multi-billionaire Arnault family, owners of the Louis Vuitton brand and Paris FC.
After opening the season with a goalless draw at Troyes, the win lifted PFC into second place.
A brace from Esteban Lepaul, including a winner from the penalty spot deep into injury-time, helped Rennes up to fifth with a 3-2 win over Le Mans, for whom Louis Mafouta also grabbed two goals.

item.title: England v Pakistan second Test: Three talking points
item.description:
England thrashed Pakistan by 194 runs to win the second Test at Lord's on Sunday and so take an unbeatable 2-0 lead in a three-match campaign.
Below AFP Sport looks at three talking points that emerged as England completed their first multi-match Test series win in over a year.
Relentless Robinson
The present England management have sometimes given the impression the only thing that matters in a pace attack is sheer speed.
But Ollie Robinson has demonstrated the importance of accuracy and movement as well.
Robinson lacks the express pace and physical threat of Sussex and England team-mate Jofra Archer.
But the seamer's range of skills were on display at Lord's where, albeit helped by a green-tinged pitch, Robinson was named player-of-the-match for a haul of 8-35 that included a remarkable 4-11 in 13 overs during Pakistan's first innings.
While concerns over his fitness and questions regarding some social media posts have threatened to derail his England career, there have rarely been any doubts over the 32-year-old Robinson's talent.
In his three Tests this season the Sussex captain has taken 23 wickets at a stunningly low average of 8.34, with England skipper Joe Root saying on Sunday Robinson was "horrendous (to face) in these conditions."
Pitch problems a worry for Lord's
The way England opener Emilio Gay fell lbw for 31 to a 'pea-shooter' delivery from Pakistan paceman Mohammad Abbas was the kind of dismissal that really should not happen on the third day of a Test and certainly not at a ground that styles itself as the Home of Cricket.
For Gay, struggling to cement his place in the England side, it was a particularly cruel exit as what should be a game of skill was turned into a lottery by uneven bounce.
It was also a worrying sign for Marylebone Cricket Club, the owners of Lord's.
The pitch for the previous Test at Lord's, against New Zealand, was rated as "unsatisfactory" by the International Cricket Council, with next year's World Test Championship final relocated across London to the Oval partly as a consequence.
And while previous surfaces at Lord's, renowned for its steep slope across the ground, faced criticism for being bland and too much in favour of the batsmen, clearly there are limits.
MCC recognised they had an issue after the New Zealand match, announcing the creation of "an agronomy advisory group" and a "phased pitch-relaying programme", although any benefits from may not be seen for several years and are unlikely to be of much consolation to Gay.
Shakeel salvages some batting respect for Pakistan
Pakistan have yet to make 200 so far this series, with the tourists dismissed for 171 and 135 during an innings and 103-run defeat in the first Test at Headingley before managing 110 and 194 at Lord's.
But that Pakistan, already bottom of the World Test Championship table before this latest thumping loss, at least got close to a benchmark total on Sunday was largely down to Saud Shakeel's enterprising 97.
Coming in with Pakistan in dire straits at 14-3, he initially scored briskly without taking undue risks before a flurry of thrilling boundaries, including two superb hooked sixes off fast bowler Josh Tongue took him to within sight of a hundred.
Shakeel fell just short of what would have been his fifth century in 25 Tests when he holed out off Tongue, the left-hander failing to join Abbas on the Lord's honours boards following the veteran seamer's five-wicket haul earlier Sunday.
"In the batting, we weren't up to the mark (in the first innings)," said Babar Azam, the Pakistan captain. "Saud Shakeel showed his class and dedication in the second innings."

item.title: Light to moderate rain likely across Bangladesh
item.description:
Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD) has forecast light to moderate rain across the country in the next 24 hours commencing 9am on Monday.
“Light to moderate rain or thundershowers accompanied by temporary gusty winds are likely at many places over Rangpur, Khulna, Barishal, Chattogram and Sylhet divisions and at a few places over Rajshahi, Dhaka and Mymensingh divisions with moderately heavy to heavy falls at places over the country,” the BMD said.
Teknaf recorded the country’s highest rainfall of 68mm in the 24 hours till 6am on Monday.
Day and night temperatures may fall slightly over the country.
The axis of monsoon troughs runs through Rajasthan, Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, the centre of the well-marked low to Assam across southern Bangladesh.
Monsoon is fairly active over Bangladesh and strong over the North Bay.
